title: Function declarations, expressions, and arrow functions
hook: JavaScript gives you three ways to write a function. The form you pick changes hoisting, the value of this, and whether the name appears in stack traces — all common interview traps.

blocks.text: A **function** is a reusable block of code you can call with arguments. JavaScript has three main syntaxes: a **function declaration** (`function foo() {}`) is hoisted with its name; a **function expression** (`const foo = function () {}`) creates a function value assigned to a variable; an **arrow function** (`const foo = () => {}`) is a shorter expression with lexical `this` and no own `arguments` object. All three are first-class — you can pass them as values, return them, and store them in variables.

entries.plainDefinition: A function defined with the function keyword at statement level. The name is hoisted to the top of its scope.
A function created as part of an expression, often assigned to a const or passed inline.
A concise function syntax introduced in ECMAScript 2015 (ES6). Captures lexical this and has no prototype property.
The engine registers declarations before running code. Function declarations are fully hoisted; const bindings are not.

blocks.text: Choosing the wrong form breaks real code. A `setTimeout` callback written as a regular function loses the class instance's `this` unless you bind it. A function expression assigned to `const` throws a ReferenceError if you call it before the line runs — unlike a declaration. Arrow functions cannot be constructors (`new` fails) and should not be used as object methods when you need dynamic `this`. Interviewers trace these differences constantly.

blocks.title: Named function expressions help debugging
blocks.body: A named expression like `const fn = function helper() {}` shows `helper` in stack traces. Anonymous arrows often appear as `(anonymous)` unless you assign them to a named const.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Parse the form
items.body: The engine distinguishes declaration (statement), expression (value), and arrow (lexical this).

items.title: Hoist or bind
items.body: Declarations register the function object early. const/let bindings enter the Temporal Dead Zone until initialized.

items.title: Create the function object
items.body: Each form produces a callable object with [[Environment]] linking to the outer lexical scope.

items.title: Invoke
items.body: Calling pushes a frame on the call stack. this binding rules differ by form (covered in later modules).

snippet.label: Declaration hoisting vs const expression
snippet.explanation: Line 1: function declaration is hoisted, so the call succeeds. Line 7: const is not hoisted for use; calling before line 8 throws ReferenceError.

snippet.label: Arrow concise bodies and implicit return
snippet.explanation: Line 1: single expression returns implicitly. Line 3: block body needs explicit return. Line 7: parentheses around object literal prevent parser from treating {} as a block.

snippet.label: Regular function vs arrow as object method
snippet.explanation: Line 4: callback is a regular function; this inside is not timer. Line 8: arrow captures lexical this from startArrow, which is timer.

blocks.title: Using arrow as a constructor
blocks.body: Arrow functions have no [[Construct]] internal method. `new MyArrow()` throws TypeError. Use a function declaration or class for constructors.

blocks.title: Arrow as prototype method when you need this
blocks.body: Placing an arrow on a prototype binds lexical this at definition time, not at call time. Use regular function syntax for instance methods that rely on dynamic this.

interviewTakeaways: Function declarations are fully hoisted; const/let function expressions are not — calling before the line throws ReferenceError.
Arrow functions capture lexical this and have no arguments object; regular functions get dynamic this from the call site.
Implicit return works only for arrow expression bodies; object literals need wrapping parentheses.
60s: Three forms — declaration (hoisted), expression (value), arrow (lexical this). Pick arrow for callbacks needing outer this; regular function for methods and constructors.
Follow-up: why does an arrow on a class field behave differently from a method shorthand?
commonPitfalls: Saying all functions hoist — only declarations hoist; const fn = function() is in the Temporal Dead Zone until initialized.
Using arrow functions everywhere including object methods that need dynamic this — classic setTimeout bug.
Strong answer: 'Declaration for hoisting and named recursion. Expression when assigning conditionally. Arrow when lexical this matters and you do not need arguments or new.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript adds parameter and return types to any form: `const f: (n: number) => number = (n) => n * 2`. At runtime it is plain JavaScript.
C# local functions are named and hoisted within their enclosing method. JavaScript has no local function statement — use nested declarations or const arrows.
